title: Land It Well, Dewi!
tag: An anime comic about the Cloud Adoption Framework and the Well-Architected Framework

cast.name: Dewi
cast.bio: Solution engineer at Contoso, put in charge of the cloud adoption work. Always asks: "Where does it say that?"

cast.name: Bayu
cast.bio: Leads Contoso's platform team. The navigator: he teaches the Cloud Adoption Framework and builds the landing zone.

cast.name: Sora
cast.bio: Workload architect who runs Well-Architected reviews. Five gems on her bracelet, one per pillar.

cast.name: Pip
cast.bio: The platform team's little cloud drone. Carries messages, and the packets in every diagram.

cast.name: Ratna
cast.bio: Contoso's chief executive. She sets the mission, and the next voyage.

villains.name: Vague
villains.what: Fuzzy goals: "move to the cloud because everyone does".
villains.beat: CAF Strategy: motivations, mission, measurable objectives

villains.name: Sprawl
villains.what: Ungoverned subscriptions, untagged resources, rules nobody enforces.
villains.beat: CAF Govern: guardrails with Azure Policy

villains.name: Open Hatch
villains.what: Public endpoints, reused passwords, secrets in code.
villains.beat: CAF Secure and the WAF Security pillar

villains.name: Lone Point
villains.what: The single point of failure: one server, one zone, one copy.

villains.name: Coin Gobbler
villains.what: Idle VMs, oversized plans, forgotten test environments.

villains.name: Snowflake
villains.what: Hand-patched servers that nobody can rebuild.
villains.beat: WAF Operational Excellence: IaC and safe deployments

villains.name: Bottleneck
villains.what: Everything squeezed through one narrow path.
villains.beat: WAF Performance Efficiency: caching and autoscale

eps.title: The Server Room Is Full
eps.sub: Why Contoso needs two frameworks, not one

beats.v: serverroom
Contoso HQ, Jakarta · the server room, basement level
Contoso runs its online shop, its warehouse and its people systems from one small server room. Tonight it's very warm in here.
BZZT!
Rack three is sparking again!
The datacenter lease ends soon, online orders keep climbing, and every fix means another late night...
Something taps on the little window. A fluffy white cloud is hovering outside. A cloud with a propeller.
prologue
Pip! Delivery for Dewi!
A flying... cloud? Carrying a map?
Pip! Message from Bayu: "Boardroom, level 30. Bring your questions."
boardroom
Contoso HQ · boardroom, level 30
Thank you for coming. Contoso is moving to Azure. Not one server at a time on weekends: the whole company, step by step, with a plan.
The whole company?
Dewi, you'll lead the adoption work with our platform team. Bayu runs that team. Sora reviews the design of every workload we build.
Welcome aboard! Think of it as a voyage for the whole fleet. Every voyage needs a map.
And every ship needs a sound design. That's two different jobs, so there are two frameworks.
Two frameworks?

items.t: decision makers responsible for Azure adoption.
the organization's whole journey, in seven phases: Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure, Manage.
Learn says "an Azure landing zone and operational standards".
the team that designs and runs a workload.
: app resources, code, AI models, data and infrastructure that work together for a business outcome.
Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency.

r.t: Where they meet: CAF builds the landing zone and the rules. Workload teams deploy into a workload landing zone and use WAF to design what goes in it.

beats.v: The Cloud Adoption Framework, CAF, is the map for the whole journey: why we go, how we plan, how we prepare Azure, then how we move, govern, secure and manage.
The Well-Architected Framework, WAF, is the shipwright's guide. It helps a workload team design one workload well, across five pillars.
So CAF is for the whole fleet... and WAF is for each ship?
That's our picture of it. In Azure terms, the harbor where the ships land is called an Azure landing zone.
d-two
Okay. One habit before we start: whenever you tell me something, I'll ask "where does it say that?"
Perfect. Every lesson card in this story links to the Microsoft Learn page it comes from.

beats.q: The shop team asks: "How do we keep our web app running if one datacenter in the Azure region fails?" Which framework answers that first?

opts.t: The Cloud Adoption Framework, because it covers the whole company
The Well-Architected Framework, because it guides the design of one workload
Neither. That's only an Azure Policy setting

beats.ex: Reliability is one of WAF's five pillars, and WAF guides the design of a single workload. CAF guides the organization-wide adoption journey.

beats.v: Pip! Part 1: the Cloud Adoption Framework. Fasten your seatbelts!
boardroom
Boardroom · the next morning
First stop on the CAF map: Strategy.
Before we touch Azure, we answer one question: why are we moving?
Because the server room keeps sparking?
A gray fog seeps under the door. It's Vague, the spirit of fuzzy goals.
Just "go to the cloud"! Everyone is doing it! Details later~
That's Vague. "Move because everyone does" is how cloud projects drift for years.

d.t: Why are we adopting Azure, and how will we measure success?
Start small. Core members typically include IT, finance and security.
Leadership buy-in, aligned strategies, operating-model readiness, partners.
Check it through four lenses: cost efficiency, resiliency, security, sustainability.

r.t: Learn: "Align technology decisions to business outcomes." Strategy is revisited, not written once.

beats.v: Here are our motivations. Fewer outages from old hardware. Faster launches for new shop features. And later, AI to help our customer service team.
Good. Learn groups motivations into three buckets: reduce business risk, accelerate innovation, and enhance agility and efficiency.
So "fewer outages" is reducing business risk, "faster launches" is agility, and "AI" is innovation?
You've got it. Then we write a mission, and objectives we can measure.

d.t: Contoso: aging hardware, a datacenter lease that's ending
Contoso: AI for customer service, later
Contoso: ship new shop features faster

items.t: gives direction and purpose. Learn frames it with three questions: why, what and how.
must be measurable. Learn suggests OKRs or KPIs to gauge progress.

r.t: The three motivation groups come from Learn. Contoso's examples are fictional.

beats.v: Our mission: serve every Contoso customer reliably, wherever they shop.
And objectives with numbers, so we know when we've arrived.
strategy
The compass above the table glows. Vague can't survive in a room with a clear direction.
Nooo... too... specific...
boardroom
Step two: a strategy team. Learn says core members typically come from IT, finance and security. Start small and grow it.
Step three: prepare the organization, so leaders, teams and partners pull in the same direction.
Step four: inform the strategy through four lenses: cost efficiency, resiliency, security and sustainability.
d-strategy
And once it's written, we're done with strategy?
No. Learn says plainly: "Strategy isn't a one-time exercise." We'll come back to it.

beats.q: Ratna wants Azure so Contoso can use AI in customer service. Which CAF motivation group is that?
beats.ex: Learn lists AI under "Accelerate innovation": access to cutting-edge AI capabilities.

eps.title: Count Every Crate
eps.sub: CAF Plan: operating model, skills, inventory, the eight strategies

beats.v: planroom
Project room, level 12
Phase 2: Plan. Learn says a cloud adoption plan "converts your cloud strategy into an actionable plan".
Five steps. Let's walk them.

d.t: Centralized, shared management or decentralized: who owns the platform, who owns workloads?
Azure adoption fundamentals, environment management, cloud-native development.
Discover inventory → select migration strategies → assess workloads.
An architecture plan gives the context for total cost of ownership (TCO).
One source of truth. Learn offers migration and cloud-native plan templates.

beats.v: Step one, the operating model. Who runs what?
Learn describes three: centralized, shared management and decentralized. We'll use shared management: a platform team for the shared foundation, workload teams for their own apps.
That split matters later. The workload teams are the people I review designs with.
Step two, skills.
Azure adoption fundamentals, environment management and cloud-native development. Plus a learning sandbox where people can practice safely.
Step three: plan the migration. And that starts with counting every crate.
Pip! Inventory scan starting!
Azure Migrate provides free discovery for on-premises and cloud environments. Discover first, decide later.
Twelve workloads! Including an old fax gateway nobody has used for years.

rows.t: Turn off what no longer adds business value
Like-for-like move. Only if it won't need changes for 2+ years
Modern hosting platform, minimal code changes
Better code structure, no new features
Redesign the architecture for scale and agility
Use a commercial SaaS product instead
Keep it where it is, for now

r.t: Learn: "Each workload can be Retired, Retained, Rehosted, Replatformed, Refactored, Rearchitected, Rebuilt, or Replaced."

beats.v: plan
Fax gateway: retire. The shop: replatform, so we stop patching its servers. The HR portal: replace it with a SaaS product.
And the warehouse system that has to stay next to the scanners? Retain it for now.
planroom
One warning from Learn: rehost only makes sense if the workload stays as it is for at least two years.
d-plan
Then we assess each workload properly. Components, dependencies, requirements.
Right. Step four: estimate costs. The Azure pricing calculator prices each service. Step five: document it all.
Learn calls the adoption plan a single source of truth for all decisions.
So by the end of Plan, we have a cloud adoption roadmap!

beats.q: The shop needs a modern hosting platform, but the team wants only small code changes. Which strategy fits?
beats.ex: Learn: replatforming "moves workloads to a modern hosting environment with minimal code changes."

eps.title: Build the Harbor
eps.sub: CAF Ready: Azure landing zones, design areas, management groups

beats.v: ready
The sky harbor · platform balcony (our picture of Azure)
Phase 3: Ready. Before the first ship arrives, the harbor has to be built.
Learn: "The Ready phase of the Cloud Adoption Framework helps you design your Azure landing zone."
It's huge! Do we build one of these for every app?
harbor
No. Learn says most organizations should have only one platform landing zone per Microsoft Entra tenant.

kicker.t: Ready · what is a landing zone?

title.t: An Azure landing zone has two parts

items.t: The centralized foundation: governance, security and shared resources for all workloads.
Where workload teams deploy and run their workloads, inside the platform's guardrails.
Learn renamed these from "application landing zones" (October 2026).

r.t: Learn's definition: "a proven and flexible architecture for governing, securing, and scaling" a multi-subscription Azure environment.

beats.v: So the hub in the middle, with the tower, is the platform landing zone... and every dock is a workload landing zone?
That's our picture. The platform team runs the hub. Each workload team runs its own dock, inside the platform's guardrails.
Small naming note: in October 2026 Learn renamed "application landing zones" to "workload landing zones". Same idea, new name.

t.t: Azure billing and Microsoft Entra tenant

d.t: Billing offer and tenant setup
Who can do what, and how they prove it
Management groups, subscriptions, naming, tags
Hub-and-spoke or Virtual WAN, hybrid links, DNS
Security operations and controls for the platform
Monitoring, operations, backup and recovery
Automated auditing and enforcement of policies
Deploy and run the platform as code

beats.v: We designed all eight areas before we poured any concrete. Billing and tenant, identity, resource organization, network, security, management, governance, and platform automation.
Resource organization starts with management groups: containers for subscriptions, arranged as a tree.
d-mg
So a policy assigned near the top flows down to every subscription below it?
Yes. Learn: governance applied to a management group cascades by inheritance to all its subscriptions.
And it's an explicit deny system. You can't loosen a parent's deny with a softer policy lower down. You exclude the child scope instead.
Corp, Online, Local... how do we choose where a workload lives?

title.t: Which management group fits a workload?

rows.t: need corporate or hybrid connectivity through the hub in the connectivity subscription
might need direct internet inbound or outbound traffic, or no virtual network at all
are experiments: isolated from Corp and Online, with a less restrictive set of policies
are canceled landing zones. Azure deletes them after 30–60 days

r.t: Learn's newest landing zone page groups Corp, Online and Local under a "Workload landing zones" management group. Older pages call it "Landing zones".

beats.v: Here's how we'll use it: the internal order API needs our corporate network, so Corp. The public shop takes traffic straight from the internet, so Online.
And the Sandbox is where people learn without breaking anything!

beats.q: A policy with a deny effect is assigned at the Contoso management group. A team wants a softer rule in its own subscription below. What does Learn say?

opts.t: Assign a looser policy at the subscription. The lowest scope wins
Azure Policy is an explicit deny system. Exclude the child scope instead of assigning a looser policy
Move the subscription to the tenant root group

beats.ex: Assignments cascade down the tree, and a looser child assignment can't override a parent's deny.

eps.title: Roads, Gates and Docks
eps.sub: CAF Ready: hub-and-spoke networking and subscription vending

beats.v: harbor
The sky harbor · central hub
A harbor needs roads. In Azure, the roads are virtual networks.
The most common shape is hub-and-spoke. Shared services live in the hub virtual network. Each workload gets its own spoke, peered to the hub.
Like our harbor: a hub in the middle, docks around it.

items.t: : inspects traffic and is the primary egress point from the spokes to the internet.
: hybrid name resolution, with inbound and outbound endpoints.

r.t: The hubs live in the Connectivity subscription (Platform → Connectivity management group). Peering isn't transitive, so spoke-to-spoke traffic needs routes through the firewall, or direct peering.

beats.v: d-hub
Wait. Spoke A can't talk to spoke B directly?
Learn: peering isn't transitive. So routes send spoke-to-spoke traffic through Azure Firewall, or you peer the spokes directly.
And notice where Application Gateway is NOT: Learn says don't deploy Layer 7 inbound appliances like it as a shared hub service. It belongs in the workload's spoke.
There's another option, Azure Virtual WAN, a Microsoft-managed hub. CAF suggests it for more than 30 branch sites, VPN-to-ExpressRoute transit, or more than two regions.
Now, how does a workload team get its own dock?
vending
Subscription vending! Learn: a platform mechanism for programmatically issuing subscriptions to workload teams.
An official front door for new docks!
harbor
d-vend
So the shop team fills in a form, and the pipeline does the rest: subscription, management group, network peering, access, budget.
And that budget isn't a hard limit. The workload team keeps it up to date.

title.t: How to build the landing zone

items.t: the platform landing zone accelerator with
The infrastructure-as-code accelerator runs in four phases: 0 Planning, 1 Prerequisites, 2 Bootstrap, 3 Run.
the Azure platform landing zone portal accelerator.
Learn's journey has three on-ramps: Start (new), Align (existing) and Enhance.

beats.q: In a hub-and-spoke design, where does traffic from a spoke go when it heads to the internet?

opts.t: Straight out of each spoke's own public IP
Through Azure Firewall in the hub, the primary egress point

beats.ex: The hub firewall sits between every spoke and the internet, on-premises and other spokes routed through it.

eps.title: The Great Migration
eps.sub: CAF Adopt: migrate, modernize, build cloud-native

beats.v: adopt
Contoso rooftop · launch day
Phase 4: Adopt. Time to move workloads, improve them, or build new ones.
Adopt has three tracks in CAF: migration, modernization and cloud-native.
And the harbor is ready for the first ships!
harbor

d.t: 1 Plan → 2 Prepare → 3 Execute → 4 Optimize → 5 Decommission
1 Prepare → 2 Plan → 3 Execute → 4 Optimize
1 Plan → 2 Build → 3 Deploy → 4 Optimize

items.t: The migration plan and the cloud-native plan both list an
Two migration methods: with downtime, or with near-zero downtime.

r.t: AI isn't an Adopt track. CAF covers AI adoption as a separate scenario.

beats.v: Our first wave is small on purpose, right?
Right. Learn: start with simpler workloads to reduce risk. And always set rollback criteria and procedures before any migration.
First up: the reporting server, a rehost with Azure Migrate.
d-migrate
The test migration doesn't touch production at all?
It runs in an isolated virtual network. You test, clean up the test, then do the real migration.
After cutover we optimize, and then we decommission the old server, properly. Stakeholder approval, licenses, data, documentation.
And the shop? It's moving to App Service. Is that migration or modernization?
Modernization. Learn: migration changes where a workload runs. And "a rehost migration alone isn't modernization."
Learn's advice for modernizing: make the least amount of change needed to reach the outcome.
Small steps, clear rollback, then celebrate!
Pip! First ship has landed!

beats.q: Where does Azure Migrate run a test migration?

opts.t: In an isolated virtual network, so production isn't touched
On the source server in the datacenter

beats.ex: The VMware migration tutorial runs the test in an isolated virtual network, then cleans it up before the real migration.

eps.title: Rules of the Harbor
eps.sub: CAF Govern: guardrails with Azure Policy

beats.v: tower
The sky harbor · control tower
Phase 5: Govern. Ships arrive every week now. Without rules, the harbor turns into chaos.
Hehe! Subscriptions with no owner! Resources with no tags! Storage in any region I like!
Who is THAT?
Sprawl. He grows wherever nobody sets guardrails.
Learn: "Cloud governance is how an organization controls its use of cloud services by establishing guardrails."

d.t: Set it up before workloads are deployed.
Priority = probability × impact. Categories include compliance, security, operations, cost, data, resources and AI.
Every risk gets one or more governance policies.
Azure Policy first. Supplement it with Microsoft Defender for Cloud (security), Microsoft Purview (data) and more.
For example with the Azure governance workbook. Governance is never "finished".

r.t: After step 1, steps 2–5 repeat in a cycle.

beats.v: So first a governance team, then risks, policies, enforcement and monitoring?
And once the team exists, steps two to five repeat as a cycle.
How do we know which risk to tackle first?
Learn gives a simple formula: risk priority equals risk probability times risk impact.
And who enforces the rules?
Azure Policy. Learn calls it Azure's primary governance tool.

items.t: Learn: Azure Policy "helps to enforce organizational standards and to assess compliance at-scale".
Assign them to a scope, such as a management group. Everything below inherits them.

rows.t: Blocks a create or update that breaks the rule
Allows it, but marks it noncompliant
Adds, changes or removes properties, such as tags
Deploys a missing related resource, such as a diagnostic setting

items.t: fix existing resources that fail deployIfNotExists or modify policies.
Learn's tip: start with audit or auditIfNotExists before you enforce.

beats.v: d-policy
govern
Hey! Let me go!
Monitor first, then deny the truly risky things.
tower
Exactly Learn's advice: use a monitor-first approach, and prefer block lists over allow lists.
Money needs guardrails too. Learn's example policy: workload teams set budget alerts at the resource group level.

beats.q: Which Azure Policy effect stops a noncompliant resource from being created?
beats.ex: deny blocks the request. audit lets it through but flags it as noncompliant.

eps.title: Guards at Every Gate
eps.sub: CAF Secure: security through every phase, Zero Trust

beats.v: gate
The sky harbor · main gate
Phase 6: Secure. Security isn't one gate at the entrance. It runs through every phase.
Psst... an open hatch somewhere? A reused password? A forgotten public endpoint?
Someone is always checking, little one.
CAF's Secure methodology spans strategy, planning, readiness, adoption, governance and operations.

title.t: CAF Secure: security in every phase

d.t: Understand who does what in security
Integrate security into the adoption strategy
Plan a secure adoption
Ready a secure cloud estate
Perform the adoption securely
Securely govern the estate
Securely manage the estate

items.t: verify explicitly · use least-privilege access · assume breach (the Zero Trust overview now says "assume compromise").

beats.v: Zero Trust means "never trust, always verify"?
Learn's three principles: verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, and assume breach. The newest Zero Trust page calls that last one "assume compromise".
secure
My badge, my device, my role: all checked. And every check is logged.
Ow! That barrier is NOT open!
gate
d-zt
And how do we know we're getting better?
CAF suggests tracking secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
Incidents still happen, so CAF covers the whole lifecycle: readiness, detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident learning.

beats.q: Which one is NOT one of the three Zero Trust principles named on Learn?
beats.ex: Zero Trust drops the idea of a trusted internal network. Every request is verified explicitly.

eps.title: The Control Tower
eps.sub: CAF Manage: Ready, Administer, Monitor, Protect

beats.v: tower
Control tower · night shift
Phase 7: Manage. The ships are flying. Now someone has to keep watch.
CAF Manage follows RAMP: Ready, Administer, Monitor, Protect.

d.t: Agree on central (platform) and workload responsibilities. Plan for change, the major cause of failure.
Change, security, compliance, data, costs, code and resources.
Azure Monitor as the main monitoring solution. Service health at the very least.
Reliability and security: backup, disaster recovery, resilient traffic routing.

beats.v: "Ready operations" means agreeing who handles what?
Central platform responsibilities and workload responsibilities. And Learn warns: "Change is the major cause of failure in the cloud."
manage
Pip! Pip! CPU alert on the reporting VM!
I see it. The alert came through exactly the way we designed it.
tower
d-monitor
Logs from every resource land in one workspace, the alert fires, and the action group wakes up the on-call engineer.
Learn: use Azure Monitor as your main monitoring solution. And monitoring service health is the bare minimum.
Then Protect: reliability and security. Azure Backup for restores, Azure Site Recovery for disaster recovery.

items.t: Learn's example: an uptime target (SLO) of
less than 52 minutes of downtime a year
Tools Learn names for protection include
, plus Azure Front Door and Traffic Manager for resilient routing.

beats.v: Fifty-two minutes a year? That's less than one long lunch!
That's why targets come from the business, not from guesswork.
Part 1 complete. Contoso has a map, a harbor, rules, guards and a control tower. Next, Sora teaches how to build each ship.

beats.q: In the RAMP approach of CAF Manage, what does the "M" stand for?
beats.ex: RAMP is Ready, Administer, Monitor, Protect.

eps.title: The Five Pillars
eps.sub: WAF: workloads, pillars, tradeoffs and the review loop

beats.v: waf
Sora's atelier
Part 2: the Well-Architected Framework. One workload at a time.
Learn defines WAF as "a set of quality-driven tenets, architectural decision points, and review tools".
And what exactly counts as a workload?
pillars
Application resources, custom code, AI models, data and supporting infrastructure that work together to achieve business outcomes. Our shop is one workload.

d.t: Resiliency, availability and recovery: meet uptime and recovery targets.
Protect confidentiality, integrity and availability, with a Zero Trust approach.
Keep spending within budget and get the most value from it.
Observability, automation and safe deployments: DevOps practices.
Adjust to changing demand efficiently: scalability, load testing.

beats.v: Then let's make the shop score a hundred on all five!
Careful. Every choice trades something. More replicas raise reliability, and cost. Deeper inspection raises security, and latency.
Learn: "The design decisions must be balanced across all pillars, given the business requirements."

items.t: has design principles, a design review checklist, tradeoffs, design patterns and a maturity model.
help you choose and configure individual Azure services (App Service, Application Gateway, SQL Database...).
covers special workloads: AI, SaaS, mission-critical, HPC, sustainability, Microsoft Fabric.
the Azure Well-Architected Review (free) and Azure Advisor.

r.t: Learn: WAF "often references Azure landing zones, but it isn't dependent on a specific platform implementation".

beats.v: How do we check our design honestly?
The Azure Well-Architected Review: a free self-assessment. And Azure Advisor scores real resources by the same five pillars.
d-review
Pip! Review loop: answer, fix, repeat!
Exactly. Now, pillar by pillar. And each pillar comes with a villain.

beats.q: Azure Advisor score is split into categories. What do they represent?

opts.t: The eight landing zone design areas

beats.ex: Learn: "The score for each category of Advisor represents each of the five pillars" of WAF.

eps.title: When an Engine Fails
eps.sub: WAF Reliability: zone redundancy, health probes, recovery

beats.v: engine
Airship engine room
Pillar 1: Reliability.
One server! One zone! One copy of everything! What could possibly go wrong?
Everything, the moment you trip. Meet Lone Point: the single point of failure.

d.t: Set clear, documented goals, negotiated with business stakeholders.
Keep working, fully or in a reduced mode, when parts fail.
Anticipate failures and recover with minimal disruption.
Shift left: anticipate failure conditions, observe, learn.
Avoid overengineering the design, the code and the operations.

beats.v: Design for business requirements comes first?
Yes. Agree measurable targets with the business before buying redundancy. Otherwise you over-build, or under-build.
reliability
One engine pod is smoking... and we're still flying!
That's redundancy. Learn: "Availability zones are physically independent datacenters or datacenter sectors" within a region.
Waaah! Nobody depends on me anymore!
engine
d-zones
Learn: "For many production workloads, a zone-redundant deployment provides the best balance of trade-offs." Mission-critical workloads use multiple zones and multiple regions.

rows.t: Identify and rate user and system flows
Plan a timely, reliable scaling strategy

beats.v: And what does all this cost us?
More replicas mean more cost, and more surface area to secure. Replication can add latency. Reliability is never free, so we match it to the target.

beats.q: Zone 1 fails. The shop runs App Service instances in zones 1, 2 and 3 behind a zone-redundant Application Gateway. What happens?

opts.t: Health probes find the unhealthy instance and traffic flows to zones 2 and 3
The whole shop is down until zone 1 recovers
Traffic automatically moves to another Azure region

beats.ex: Zone redundancy keeps capacity in other zones, and health probes route around unhealthy instances. Surviving a whole-region outage needs a multi-region design.

eps.title: Lock Every Hatch
eps.sub: WAF Security: one public door, private everything else

beats.v: gate
Beneath the harbor · the private passage
Pillar 2: Security.
I'm back! Surely ONE storage account still allows public access...
Not in this design. In Learn's baseline web app, SQL Database, Storage and Key Vault all block public access.

d.t: A readiness plan aligned with business priorities.
Prevent exposure of private, regulated and proprietary information.
Prevent corruption of the design, implementation, operations and data.
Minimize downtime and degradation during a security incident.

t.t: Sustain and evolve your security posture

d.t: Your security posture must not degrade over time.

r.t: Zero Trust: verify explicitly · use least-privilege access · assume breach ("assume compromise" on the newest Zero Trust page).

beats.v: Where does Zero Trust fit into WAF?
Learn is direct: "A Well-Architected workload must be built with a zero-trust approach."
security
One public door, a guard at that door, and private passages behind it.
And keys that only open the doors you need. That's least privilege.
gate
d-sec
The Application Gateway is the only public entry. The WAF blocks bad requests. Everything else travels over private endpoints.
And no passwords in code: the app uses a managed identity to read secrets from Key Vault.

rows.t: Strict, conditional, auditable identity and access
Isolate, filter and control network traffic

beats.v: Any downsides?
Security adds cost, and some latency from extra checks. And a WAF tuned for languages you don't even use just slows things down. Tune it to your workload.
Hmph. Fine. I'll find an easier target...

beats.q: In the baseline web app, how does App Service reach Azure SQL Database?

opts.t: Over the public internet, with a firewall rule
Through VNet integration and a private endpoint, resolved by a private DNS zone

beats.ex: Outbound flow: VNet integration routes the call, the linked private DNS zone returns the private endpoint IP, and the virtual network delivers it through the private endpoint.

eps.title: Fuel Wisely
eps.sub: WAF Cost Optimization: budgets, Advisor, rates and right-sizing

beats.v: engine
Engine room · the fuel deck
Pillar 3: Cost Optimization.
Om nom nom! Idle VMs! Oversized plans! Forgotten test environments! Delicious!
He's eating our budget!
Learn has a line I love: "A cost-optimized workload isn't necessarily a low-cost workload." It's about value for the money.

d.t: The whole team knows the budget, the spending and the reports.
Spend only on what returns value.
Get full use out of what you already pay for.
Pay a lower rate for the same thing, without redesigning.
Keep right-sizing as the workload evolves.

beats.v: cost
Step one: know where the money goes!
Budgets in Microsoft Cost Management alert on actual or forecasted cost. But they don't stop anything. A person or automation has to act.
engine
d-cost
Right-size first, then commit. Discounts reduce rates, not waste!
Those are almost Learn's exact words. Reservations for stable, always-on workloads. Savings plans for dynamic or evolving ones.

title.t: Cost Optimization checklist: CO:01 to CO:14

rows.t: Create a culture of financial responsibility
Create and maintain a cost model
Get the best rates from providers

beats.v: And the tradeoff: hard spending limits can stop a workload from scaling for real demand. Aggressive scale-in can leave it unprepared.
Urp... nothing left to eat...

beats.q: A Cost Management budget reaches 100% of its amount. What happens to the resources?

opts.t: Nothing. The budget sends alerts, and the resources keep running
They move to a cheaper region

beats.ex: Learn: "Resources aren't affected, and your consumption isn't stopped." Someone, or automation, has to act on the alert.

eps.title: Same Every Time
eps.sub: WAF Operational Excellence: IaC, pipelines, safe deployments

beats.v: atelier
The atelier · the new assembly line
Pillar 4: Operational Excellence.
I'm unique! Hand-patched at 2 a.m.! Nobody remembers how to rebuild me!
Snowflake. A server configured by hand, a little different every time. Impossible to repeat.

d.t: Development and operations share ownership and keep improving together.
Standard practices, quality gates and tracked progress.
Gain visibility, derive insight, make data-driven decisions.
Replace repetitive manual tasks with software automation.
Guardrails that make releases consistent and recoverable.

beats.v: So we describe the infrastructure as code instead?

Learn: use infrastructure as code to define the desired state of all infrastructure, make changes only through code, and deploy it through CI/CD pipelines. It also helps you detect configuration drift.
opex
Every ship from the same blueprint! No snowflakes!
I'm... melting...
atelier
d-deploy
Deploy to staging, warm it up, check its health, then swap. And if something's wrong, swap straight back!
Safe deployment practices: progressive exposure, health checks before each phase, and a way to recover that you planned before you started.

title.t: Operational Excellence checklist: OE:01 to OE:11

rows.t: Define standard practices to develop and operate
Standardize routine, ad hoc and emergency operations
Use industry-standard development and QA practices
Prepare resources with standardized infrastructure as code
Drive changes through predictable, automated pipelines
Design a monitoring stack: telemetry, metrics, logs

beats.v: The tradeoff: safe deployment patterns run extra instances for a while. That costs a bit more. Usually it's worth it.

beats.q: A bad release reached production through a slot swap. What's the fastest rollback?

opts.t: Swap the same two slots again

beats.ex: Learn: you can restore the slots to their pre-swap states by swapping the same two slots immediately.

eps.title: Rush Hour
eps.sub: WAF Performance Efficiency: edge caching, cache-aside, autoscale

beats.v: harbor
The sky harbor · 12.12 sale day
Pillar 5: Performance Efficiency. It's the big 12.12 online sale, and everyone shows up at once.
Squeeeeze! Everybody through my tiny neck! One! At! A! Time!
Learn describes performance efficiency as the ability to adapt to changing demand: scale up for load, scale down when it's quiet.

d.t: Define the intended user experience and a benchmark strategy.
Provide enough supply for the expected demand.
Protect against degradation in use and as the system evolves.
Use production data to keep improving within the targets.

beats.v: perf
The docks are unfolding by themselves!
Scale out when it's busy, serve repeat requests from caches, and keep the database for the work only it can do.
My neck! It's... it's free!
harbor
d-scale
Images come from the edge, product data from the cache, and more instances join when CPU climbs.
Always set an upper limit. Learn warns that autoscaling without one can lead to uncontrolled growth, and an uncontrolled bill.

title.t: Performance Efficiency checklist: PE:01 to PE:12

rows.t: Test regularly in a production-like environment
Prioritize the performance of critical flows

beats.v: And we test before the sale, not during it.
Exactly: PE:06, test regularly in a production-like environment.
Product names matter: Learn's Cache-Aside page suggests Azure Managed Redis. Azure Cache for Redis is being retired.

beats.q: With the Cache-Aside pattern, what does the app do on a cache miss?

opts.t: Return an error and retry later
Read the data store, add the item to the cache, then return it

beats.ex: Cache-Aside loads data into the cache on demand: on a miss, read from the store, then populate the cache.

eps.title: Land It Well
eps.sub: CAF and WAF together: the shop in its landing zone

beats.v: deck
On deck · sunset over the harbor
Some months later. The shop runs in its own workload landing zone. Time to see the whole picture.
Here's the shop today: Learn's baseline zone-redundant web app, inside a workload landing zone, connected to the platform.
d-final
CAF built the harbor and its rules. WAF shaped the ship.
And who owns what is clear. Learn: Azure landing zone architectures "separate ownership between the platform team and the workload team".

title.t: The whole journey on one card

items.t: motivations, mission, objectives → team → organization → four lenses
operating model, skills, inventory and the 8 Rs, costs, plan
the Azure landing zone: platform + workload landing zones, 8 design areas
team → risks → policies → enforce → monitor (a cycle)
security in every phase, Zero Trust
Azure Well-Architected Review · Azure Advisor score · service guides

r.t: The full cheat sheet page has every step and principle name, each with its Learn source.

beats.v: And nothing here is ever really "done", is it?
No. Strategy gets revisited, governance runs as a cycle, the review gets re-run as a milestone.
Dewi, the board read your adoption plan. Next voyage: AI for customer service.
AI? Already?
CAF has an AI adoption scenario: AI strategy, AI plan and AI ready, then govern, secure and manage AI continuously. And Learn shows how AI workloads fit into the landing zone we already have.
And WAF has AI workload guidance. Same five pillars, new tradeoffs.
finale
Pip pip! Mission complete!
Semangat! Now... where does it say the next part? I'm off to read Learn!

beats.q: In an Azure landing zone, who typically owns the hub's Azure Firewall, and who owns the shop's Application Gateway?

opts.t: The platform team owns the hub. The workload team owns the Application Gateway in its spoke
Microsoft owns the hub; the platform team owns the gateway

beats.ex: Learn's landing zone baselines separate platform and workload ownership: the platform team runs the hub, and Application Gateway and its public IP live in the workload's spoke.

d-two.title: How CAF and WAF fit together

zones.label: Cloud Adoption Framework · the organization's journey

steps.c: Strategy: decide why Contoso adopts Azure and how success will be measured.
Plan: turn the strategy into an actionable plan: operating model, skills, inventory, costs.
Ready: build the Azure landing zone. The platform landing zone holds shared governance, security and services.
Adopt: migrate, modernize or build each workload into a workload landing zone.
The platform's guardrails (policies, network, identity) apply to every workload landing zone.
Inside its landing zone, each workload team designs its workload with WAF's five pillars.
Govern, Secure and Manage never stop: they run across the whole estate.

d-two.note: Our simplified picture. CAF guides the organization; WAF guides each workload inside its landing zone.

nodes.label:
Four lenses
cost · resiliency
security · sustainability

steps.c: Motivations first. Learn groups them: reduce business risk, accelerate innovation, enhance agility and efficiency.
A mission gives direction and purpose. Objectives and KPIs make progress measurable.
Define a strategy team. Core members typically come from IT, finance and security.
Prepare the organization: leadership buy-in, aligned strategies, operating-model readiness, partners.
Inform the strategy through four lenses: cost efficiency, resiliency, security, sustainability.
Then revisit it. Learn: "Strategy isn't a one-time exercise."

d-plan.title: From inventory to decisions

steps.c: Discover: Azure Migrate finds servers, apps and dependencies. Learn: its discovery is free.
Assess: full visibility into every component, dependency and requirement.
Old fax gateway: no business value left → Retire.
Reporting server: no changes needed for two years or more → Rehost.
Contoso Shop: a modern platform with minimal code changes → Replatform to App Service.
HR portal: a SaaS product does the job → Replace.
Warehouse scanners must stay on site → Retain, for now.
Prioritize into migration waves. Learn: start with simpler workloads to reduce risk.

d-plan.note: Workload names and choices are Contoso's (fictional). The strategies and steps come from Learn.

d-mg.title: Management groups and policy inheritance

steps.c: An initiative is assigned at the intermediate root, Contoso. Example: the built-in "Allowed locations" policy with a deny effect.
The assignment cascades by inheritance to every child management group...
...and on down to every subscription and resource below them.
Corp: needs the corporate network through the hub. Online: may need direct internet traffic. Local: Azure Local clusters.
Sandbox: isolated from Corp and Online, with a less restrictive set of policies.
Decommissioned: canceled landing zones wait here. Azure deletes them after 30–60 days.

d-mg.note: Learn's newest page groups Corp ("Internal"), Online and Local under "Workload landing zones"; older pages say "Landing zones".

d-hub.title: Hub-and-spoke: who talks to whom

steps.c: On-premises users call the Order API: through the VPN/ExpressRoute gateway, inspected by Azure Firewall, into spoke A.
Spoke A calls the reporting VM in spoke B. Peering isn't transitive, so user-defined routes send it through the firewall.
Spoke B goes out to the internet. Azure Firewall is the primary egress point.
Admins connect through Azure Bastion: RDP or SSH over private IPs, so the VMs need no public IP.
Hybrid DNS: the DNS Private Resolver forwards queries for on-premises names toward on-premises DNS.

d-hub.note: Learn: don't deploy Layer 7 inbound appliances such as Application Gateway as a shared hub service. They belong in the workload's spoke.

d-vend.title: Subscription vending

steps.c: The shop team asks for a subscription: budget, owners, networking needs, criticality, confidentiality.
Business logic and approval come from the Cloud Center of Excellence.
The request pipeline writes a parameter file (JSON, YAML or TFVARS) and opens a pull request.
Merging triggers the deployment pipeline, which runs the Bicep or Terraform vending module.
A new subscription is created and placed in the right management group, so it inherits policy.
Then: a virtual network peered to the hub, access for the team, and a preliminary budget.
Hand-off. The workload team deploys and operates, and keeps the budget current: budgets aren't hard limits.

d-vend.note: A synthesis of Learn's CAF and Architecture Center vending pages. Your platform team's tooling may differ.

d-migrate.title: Rehost with Azure Migrate

steps.c: Discover: the Azure Migrate appliance continuously discovers servers and sends their metadata to the project.
Assess: readiness, right-sizing, cost estimates and dependencies, ready for a business case.
Replicate: initial replication, then delta replication keeps Azure in sync.
Test migration: a test VM starts in an isolated virtual network. Check it, then clean up the test.
Migrate: cut over in the workload landing zone, then complete the migration.
Optimize (Advisor, backup, alerts), then decommission the source server.

d-migrate.note: Stage names follow Learn's agentless VMware tutorial. Other sources (Hyper-V, physical) differ in detail.

d-policy.title: Azure Policy guardrails in action

steps.c: Contoso assigns an initiative at its management group. Every subscription below inherits it.
deny: a deployment to a region outside "Allowed locations". Azure Policy blocks the request.
modify: a resource arrives without its cost-center tag. "Add a tag to resources" adds it during the request.
deployIfNotExists: after a VM is created, Policy deploys the missing diagnostic setting, so logs reach Log Analytics.
audit: the resource is allowed, but it's marked noncompliant on the compliance dashboard.
Remediation tasks bring existing resources into compliance for deployIfNotExists and modify policies.

d-policy.note: "Allowed locations" (Deny) and "Add a tag to resources" (Modify) are built-in examples Learn names.

d-zt.title: Zero Trust: every request is checked

steps.c: Verify explicitly: Conditional Access brings signals together (user, device, location, risk) to make a decision.
The policy asks for MFA. Then Dewi reaches only the app her role needs: least privilege.
The app reads its secret from Key Vault with a managed identity: no credentials in the code.
A stolen password from an unknown device? Conditional Access can block the sign-in.
Assume breach: Defender for Cloud and Microsoft Sentinel, a cloud-native SIEM, collect signals to detect and respond.

d-zt.note: Learn's newest Zero Trust page calls the third principle "assume compromise" (previously "assume breach").

steps.c: Diagnostic settings send logs and metrics from each resource to one Log Analytics workspace.
An alert rule watches the data, for example CPU above a threshold. When its condition is met, the alert fires.
The alert triggers an action group: email, SMS, push or voice, or actions such as runbooks and webhooks.
Protect: Azure Backup stores recovery points in a Recovery Services vault.
Protect: Azure Site Recovery replicates the VM to a secondary region, ready for failover and failback.
The team takes the Azure Well-Architected Review: free, about 60 questions across the five pillars.
It can pull in Azure Advisor recommendations for the workload's resources.
Export the recommendations to CSV and add them to the workload backlog.
Fix, deploy, repeat.
Advisor score rises. Each category score represents one pillar, refreshed at least once a day.
Use the assessment's milestones to re-run the review and track progress over time.

d-zones.title: Zone redundancy: losing a zone, not the shop

steps.c: A normal day: Application Gateway spreads requests across App Service instances in three availability zones.
Health probes: Application Gateway checks every back-end instance, and App Service health check watches them too.
Zone 1 has an outage. Its instance fails the health checks and is taken out of rotation.
Requests flow to the healthy instances in zones 2 and 3. Customers keep shopping.
The zone-redundant database keeps serving. For zone-redundant resources, Microsoft manages zone failover automatically.
Zone 1 recovers and its instance rejoins. Learn's advice: overprovision so the remaining zones can carry the load.

d-zones.note: A single-region design. Surviving the loss of a whole region needs a multi-region design.

d-sec.title: Baseline web app: one public door

steps.c: A shopper connects over HTTPS to Application Gateway, the single public entry point. Its TLS certificate lives in Key Vault.
An attacker sends a SQL injection. In Prevention mode, the WAF blocks attacks its rules detect.
A private DNS zone resolves the App Service name to its private endpoint, and the gateway forwards the request privately.
App Service reads a secret from Key Vault: DNS returns the private endpoint IP, and a managed identity proves who's asking.
Orders go to SQL Database and files to Storage, each through a private endpoint.
A direct call from the internet to the database? SQL Database, Storage and Key Vault all block public access.

d-sec.note: Simplified from Learn's "Baseline highly available zone-redundant web application": the private endpoints of Key Vault, SQL Database and Storage appear as labels on the arrows, and App Service's VNet integration subnet isn't drawn.

steps.c: Usage and cost data flow into Microsoft Cost Management.
A budget compares actual and forecasted cost with its thresholds (up to five).
A threshold is crossed: the cost alert notifies the team. The resources keep running.
Azure Advisor spots an underutilized VM: right-size it, or shut it down.
Stable, always-on usage? A reservation lowers the rate.
Dynamic or evolving usage? A savings plan. Right-size first: discounts reduce rates, not waste.

d-deploy.title: Infrastructure as code and a safe slot swap

steps.c: A change is merged. The pipeline builds and tests it automatically.
Infrastructure as code (Bicep) applies the desired state, then the app deploys to the staging slot.
App Service warms up each staging instance with a request to the app root before the swap.
Health checks pass, so swap: the slots switch routing rules and no requests are dropped.
Shoppers get the new version while Application Insights watches it.
Something's wrong? Swap the same two slots again. That's an immediate rollback.

d-scale.title: Rush hour: edge cache, cache-aside, autoscale

steps.c: Shoppers ask for product images. The Front Door edge has a cached copy: served from the edge, no trip to the origin.
Not cached yet? The edge forwards the request to the origin, App Service, and caches the response (GET requests only).
Product data: the app checks Azure Managed Redis first. Cache hit: a fast answer.
Cache miss: read SQL Database, add the item to the cache, return it. That's the Cache-Aside pattern.
CPU above 70%: Azure Monitor autoscale adds an instance, never above the maximum you set.
The sale ends and CPU drops below 40%: autoscale removes the extra instance to save cost.

d-scale.note: CPU thresholds follow the example on Learn's autoscale overview (add above 70%, remove below 40%).

d-final.title: The shop in its landing zone

zones.label: Workload landing zone: Contoso Shop · shop team

steps.c: Shoppers reach Application Gateway + WAF in the shop's spoke. It forwards privately to zone-redundant App Service.
App Service uses Key Vault, SQL Database and Storage over private endpoints.
Calls to services outside Azure leave through the hub's Azure Firewall, over the hub-spoke peering.
Application Insights and diagnostic settings send telemetry to the central Log Analytics workspace.
Azure Policy, assigned at the management groups, keeps the spoke inside the guardrails.
The platform team owns the hub and shared services. The shop team owns everything in its spoke.

d-final.note: Combines Learn's baseline zone-redundant web app with the landing zone split of platform and workload teams. Simplified.
